o: We need the shortest string containing both s1 and s2 as substrings. First, if one string already contains the other, the longer string is the answer (Example 2: "aa" is inside "aaa"). Otherwise the best we can do is overlap a suffix of one string with a prefix of the other; the answer is either s1 followed by the non-overlapping tail of s2, or vice versa (Example 1: "aba"+"bab" overlaps "ab", giving "abab"). With lengths ≤ 100, checking every possible overlap length is trivially fast.
k: If one string contains the other, that string alone is optimal.
Otherwise the optimal superstring is one string plus the tail of the other after their maximum suffix/prefix overlap.
Only two merge orientations exist (s1+s2, s2+s1); try both and take the shorter.

a.n: Approach 1: Best overlap in both directions
a.i: For an ordered pair (a, b), the merged string a+b loses the longest k such that the last k characters of a equal the first k of b. Trying all k from large to small finds the maximum overlap; doing this for both orders and taking the shorter result is optimal, because any superstring of two strings must contain one of these two merge structures or be longer.
s: Handle containment: if b occurs in a, return a (and vice versa).
For each order, scan overlap lengths k from min(len) down to 1; if a ends with b's first k chars, return a + b[k:].
If no overlap exists, return simple concatenation.
Return the shorter of the two merged candidates.
a.t: O(n·m) — for each of two orders we test up to min(n,m) overlap lengths with substring comparisons

w: This two-orientation greedy merge is provably optimal for two strings: any common superstring shorter than both merges would require a longer shared region than the maximum overlap, which is impossible. Pitfalls: forgetting the containment check (it is implied by the overlap loop only partially) and forgetting to try both orders. Follow-up: for k strings this becomes the classic Traveling-Salesman-style bitmask DP (LeetCode 943).
